claim: Extended night or rotating shift work is associated with an elevated risk for developing cancer, cardiovascular disease, immune deficiency, mood disorders, and metabolic alterations.
source: Extended night or rotating shift work is associated with an elevated risk for developing cancer, cardiovascular disease, immune deficiency, mood disorders, and metabolic alterations (Rosenberg and Doghramji, 2011; Herichova, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rosenberg and Doghramji, 2011 and Herichova, 2013

claim: A major factor contributing to the adverse health impact of shift work is disruption of endogenous circadian clocks by mistimed resetting stimuli as a consequence of altered sleep/wake schedules.
source: One major factor believed to contribute to this adverse health impact of shift work is a disruption of endogenous circadian clocks by mistimed resetting stimuli, so called Zeitgebers, as a consequence of altered sleep/wake schedules.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of circadian biology and shift work effects

claim: Circadian clocks in mammals are based on ubiquitously expressed cellular interlocking transcriptional–translational feedback loops (TTLs) of clock genes/proteins.
source: In mammals, these so called circadian clocks are based on ubiquitously expressed cellular interlocking transcriptional–translational feedback loops (TTLs) of clock genes/proteins (Albrecht, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albrecht, 2012

claim: In the core TTL, CLOCK and BMAL1 regulate the expression of two Cryptochrome (Cry1/2) and three Period (Per1-3) genes.
source: In the core TTL, the transcriptional activators circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) and brain and muscle ARNT-like 1 (BMAL1; ARNTL) regulate the expression of two Cryptochrome (Cry1/2) and three Period (Per1-3) genes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of circadian clock molecular mechanisms

claim: Towards the end of the day, PER and CRY proteins translocate into the nucleus where they inhibit their own abundance via inhibition of CLOCK/BMAL1.
source: Towards the end of the day, PER and CRY proteins translocate into the nucleus where they inhibit their own abundance via inhibition of CLOCK/BMAL1.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of circadian clock molecular mechanisms

claim: The clock machinery regulates physiology via orchestration of tissue-specific rhythmic expression of clock output genes.
source: The clock machinery regulates physiology via orchestration of tissue-specific rhythmic expression of clock output genes (Yan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yan et al., 2008

claim: The external light–dark cycle is the most prominent Zeitgeber of the central circadian pacemaker located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus.
source: The external light–dark cycle is the most prominent Zeitgeber of the central circadian pacemaker located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus (Golombek and Rosenstein, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Golombek and Rosenstein, 2010

claim: The SCN receives light information from the retina and synchronizes peripheral clocks throughout the body via neuronal and hormonal pathways.
source: The SCN receives light information from the retina and synchronizes peripheral clocks throughout the body via neuronal and hormonal pathways (Dibner et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dibner et al., 2010

claim: The SCN itself is largely non-responsive to non-photic timing signals such as food intake.
source: While the SCN itself is largely non-responsive to non-photic timing signals such as food intake, meal timing is an important Zeitgeber for clocks in peripheral tissues (Stokkan et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stokkan et al., 2001

claim: Meal timing is an important Zeitgeber for clocks in peripheral tissues.
source: While the SCN itself is largely non-responsive to non-photic timing signals such as food intake, meal timing is an important Zeitgeber for clocks in peripheral tissues (Stokkan et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stokkan et al., 2001

claim: If food access is restricted to the normal rest phase of an organism, peripheral clocks become uncoupled from the SCN and adapt to the timing of food availability.
source: If food access is restricted to the normal rest phase of an organism, that is, the night for humans or daytime for nocturnal rodents, peripheral clocks become uncoupled from the SCN and adapt to the timing of food availability (Damiola et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damiola et al., 2000

claim: Shift workers often eat at times when their digestive timing system is poorly prepared for food.
source: Shift workers often eat at times when their digestive timing system is poorly prepared for food (Lowden et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lowden et al., 2010

claim: Food intake during the normal rest phase promotes obesity in animal studies.
source: Animal studies suggest that food intake during the normal rest phase promotes obesity (Arble et al., 2009; Hatori et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Arble et al., 2009 and Hatori et al., 2012

claim: Peripheral circadian uncoupling has been suggested to contribute to the development of metabolic disorders in night shift workers.
source: peripheral circadian uncoupling has been suggested to contribute to the development of metabolic disorders in night shift workers (Antunes et al., 2010; Barclay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Antunes et al., 2010 and Barclay et al., 2012

claim: Glucocorticoids, changes in body temperature, and autonomic signaling can regulate clock gene expression in peripheral tissues.
source: Various other factors can regulate clock gene expression in peripheral tissues, including glucocorticoids and changes in body temperature or autonomic signaling (Dibner et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dibner et al., 2010

claim: The mechanisms of food-dependent peripheral clock resetting remain poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms of food-dependent peripheral clock resetting, however, remain poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Metabolic hormones such as insulin, ghrelin, and glucagon have been shown to affect circadian rhythms associated with food restriction.
source: Metabolic hormones such as insulin, ghrelin, and glucagon (GCG) have been shown to affect circadian rhythms associated with food restriction (LeSauter et al., 2009; Tahara et al., 2011; Chaves et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to LeSauter et al., 2009; Tahara et al., 2011; Chaves et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015

claim: Ghrelin appears to act primarily on the brain.
source: While ghrelin appears to act primarily on the brain, insulin and GCG levels are mainly regulated via blood glucose.
evidence: Based on inference from the literature context

claim: Insulin and GCG levels are mainly regulated via blood glucose.
source: While ghrelin appears to act primarily on the brain, insulin and GCG levels are mainly regulated via blood glucose.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of metabolic hormone regulation

claim: Carbohydrate intake alone has only a minor phase resetting capacity, while complex foods show much stronger effects.
source: However, it was shown that carbohydrate intake alone has only a minor phase resetting capacity, while complex foods show much stronger effects (Hirao et al., 2009), indicating that other factors must be involved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirao et al., 2009

claim: The gastrointestinal tract shows acute hormonal responses to fasting or feeding.
source: Besides the pancreas, other organs—notably including the gastrointestinal tract itself—show acute hormonal responses to fasting or feeding (Stanley et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanley et al., 2005

claim: Oxyntomodulin (OXM) is a potent resetting signal of liver circadian clocks.
source: In a screen using rhythmic liver slice cultures, we identified oxyntomodulin (OXM) as a potent resetting signal of liver circadian clocks.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the screen described in the manuscript

claim: OXM is an anorexigenic incretin hormone produced in the gut by prohormone convertase 1/3-driven cleavage of the precursor preproglucagon.
source: OXM is an anorexigenic incretin hormone produced in the gut by prohormone convertase 1/3-driven cleavage of the precursor preproglucagon (for review see Drucker, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Drucker, 2005

claim: OXM modulates energy and glucose metabolism by acting on various tissues, including brain, liver, and pancreas.
source: It modulates energy and glucose metabolism by acting on various tissues, including brain, liver, and pancreas (Baldissera et al., 1988; Gros et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baldissera et al., 1988 and Gros et al., 1993

claim: OXM secretion is dependent on food intake.
source: Since OXM secretion is dependent on food intake, we hypothesized that OXM may directly link food intake to hepatic transcriptional activity by resetting of the liver clock.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of OXM physiology

claim: Out of 200 peptides applied during the descending phase of the luciferase activity rhythm, only a few produced marked phase shifts, including three proglucagon-derived peptide (PGDP) hormones: exendin-4, OXM, and GCG.
source: Interestingly, out of 200 peptides applied during the descending phase (∼180°, corresponding to the early morning) of the luciferase activity rhythm, only a few produced marked phase shifts, including three proglucagon-derived peptide (PGDP) hormones: exendin-4, OXM, and GCG (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data from the peptide library screen

claim: Exendin-4 has been isolated from the salivary gland of the Gila monster, with no analogue in rodents or humans.
source: Exendin-4 has been isolated from the salivary gland of the Gila monster, with no analogue in rodents or humans.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of exendin-4

claim: GLP-1, GLP-2, and GRPP (0.5–450 nM) had no significant resetting effects on PER2::LUC phase compared to PBS-treatment.
source: GLP-1, GLP-2, and GRPP (0.5–450 nM) had no significant resetting effects on PER2::LUC phase compared to PBS-treatment (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: GCG resulted in phase delays of up to 3 hr, but only at relatively high concentrations.
source: GCG resulted in phase delays of up to 3 hr, but only at relatively high concentrations (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: OXM reset PER2::LUC rhythms in liver slices at much lower doses than GCG, resulting in phase delays of up to 8 hr at higher concentrations.
source: In contrast, OXM reset PER2::LUC rhythms in liver slices at much lower doses, resulting in phase delays of up to 8 hr at higher concentrations (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: DEX treatment reset PER2::LUC activity rhythms in slices in a phase-dependent manner.
source: In a phase-dependent manner DEX treatment reset PER2::LUC activity rhythms in slices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: DEX application in the first quarter of the PER2::LUC activity rhythm (0–90°) resulted in phase delays, while later treatments produced phase advances (100–180°) or had no marked effect (around 270°).
source: Very similar to what had been observed after DEX treatment in animals (Balsalobre et al., 2000), application in the first quarter of the PER2::LUC activity rhythm (0–90°) resulted in phase delays, while later treatments produced phase advances (100–180°) or had no marked effect (around 270°).
evidence: Based on experimental data and comparison to Balsalobre et al., 2000

claim: OXM effects were phase dependent, with delays predominantly observed at 90–210° of the PER2::LUC cycle with a maximum around 180°, while only modest phase shifts were seen at 270–360°.
source: Likewise, OXM effects were phase dependent. Delays were predominantly observed at 90–210° of the PER2::LUC cycle with a maximum around 180°, while only modest phase shifts were seen at 270–360° (Figure 1G).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: OXM secretion is directly induced by food consumption in humans.
source: Moreover, contrary to GCG, OXM secretion is directly induced by food consumption in humans (Le Quellec et al., 1992)
evidence: Supported by citation to Le Quellec et al., 1992

claim: No OXM-specific receptor has been identified so far.
source: So far no OXM-specific receptor has been identified; however, OXM can bind to and activate both GCG and GLP-1 receptors (Jorgensen et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge, supported by citation to Jorgensen et al., 2007

claim: OXM can bind to and activate both GCG and GLP-1 receptors.
source: So far no OXM-specific receptor has been identified; however, OXM can bind to and activate both GCG and GLP-1 receptors (Jorgensen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jorgensen et al., 2007

claim: Gcgr transcripts are strongly expressed in the murine liver.
source: Gcgr transcripts are strongly expressed in the murine liver (Sinclair et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sinclair et al., 2008

claim: The majority of previous studies failed to detect a full-length Glp1r mRNA in murine hepatocytes.
source: In contrast, the majority of previous studies failed to detect a full-length Glp1r mRNA in murine hepatocytes (Campos et al., 1994; Dunphy et al., 1998; Panjwani et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campos et al., 1994; Dunphy et al., 1998; Panjwani et al., 2013

claim: Glp1r transcripts were present in pancreas, but undetectable in liver samples.
source: Glp1r transcripts were present in pancreas, but undetectable in liver samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Based on experimental RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: OXM treatment resets PER2::LUC rhythms in slices from PER2::LUC x Glp1r−/− mice.
source: in line with the absence of significant liver clock resetting effects of GLP-1 (Figure 1B) and potent resetting of PER2::LUC rhythms by OXM treatment in slices from PER2::LUC x Glp1r−/− mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Blocking glucagon receptor (GCGR) signaling by co-treatment with GRI-2 potently inhibited GCG- and OXM-induced clock resetting in Per2::LUC slices.
source: On the other hand, blocking glucagon receptors (GCGR) signaling by co-treatment with 2-(4-Pyridyl)-5-(4-chlorophenyl)-3-(5-bromo-2-propyloxyphenyl)pyrrol (Calbiochem Glucagon Receptor Inhibitor II; GRI-2) potently inhibited GCG- and OXM-induced clock resetting in Per2::LUC slices (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: GCGR is a G protein-coupled receptor that, via protein kinase A, leads to phosphorylation and activation of the transcription factor CREB.
source: GCGR is a G protein-coupled receptor that, via protein kinase A, leads to phosphorylation and activation of the transcription factor cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) response element-binding protein (CREB) (Gonzalez and Montminy, 1989; Dalle et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gonzalez and Montminy, 1989 and Dalle et al., 2004

claim: In the SCN, nocturnal light exposure induces Per gene transcription via cAMP signaling and CREB activation downstream of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor.
source: This pathway is reminiscent of the SCN, where nocturnal light exposure induces Per gene transcription via cAMP signaling and CREB activation downstream of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (Welsh et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Welsh et al., 2010

claim: 30 min after OXM treatment, CREB binding was significantly increased at the Per1 CRE, but not at downstream sequences.
source: 30 min after OXM treatment, CREB binding was significantly increased at the Per1 CRE, but not at downstream sequences (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on experimental ChIP data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Per1 expression was transiently induced 60 min after addition of OXM to the medium, returning back to normal levels after 120 min.
source: Per1 expression was transiently induced 60 min after addition of OXM to the medium, returning back to normal levels after 120 min (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Per2 was induced by OXM after 60 min, but mRNA levels remained high even after 120 min.
source: Similarly, Per2 was induced by OXM after 60 min, but mRNA levels remained high even after 120 min (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 3B

claim: No significant effect was seen on Bmal1 expression at all time points after OXM treatment at 180°.
source: No significant effect was seen on Bmal1 expression at all time points (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Per1/2 and Bmal1 mRNA levels were unaffected by OXM treatment at 360°.
source: In line with the absence of OXM-induced phase shifts at 360° (Figure 1G), Per1/2 and Bmal1 mRNA levels were unaffected by OXM treatment at this phase (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 3D-F

claim: Induction of Per1 and Per2 expression was preserved in Glp1r−/− slices, suggesting that hepatic OXM effects are independent of GLP-1R signaling.
source: Induction of Per1 and Per2 expression was preserved in Glp1r−/− slices, suggesting that hepatic OXM effects are independent of GLP-1R signaling (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 3G,H and inference from the results

claim: Robust Per1 and Per2 induction was observed after i.v. injection of OXM at ZT3.
source: Analogous to what we observed in slices, robust Per1 and Per2 induction was observed after i.v. injection of OXM at Zeitgeber time (ZT) 3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on experimental in vivo qPCR data shown in Figure 4A

claim: When animals were treated with OXM at ZT15, no induction of Per gene expression was observed.
source: When animals were treated with OXM at the opposite phase of the LD cycle (ZT15)—a time when nocturnal mice usually eat and, thus, no food-mediated clock shifts would be expected—no induction of Per gene expression was observed (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on experimental in vivo qPCR data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In situ hybridization showed no acute effect of OXM treatment on Per expression in the SCN at ZT3.
source: Of note, in situ hybridization (ISH) showed no acute effect of OXM treatment on Per expression in the SCN at ZT3 (Figure 4C)
evidence: Based on experimental ISH data shown in Figure 4C

claim: OXM acts primarily on the liver clock and not the SCN clock.
source: Of note, in situ hybridization (ISH) showed no acute effect of OXM treatment on Per expression in the SCN at ZT3 (Figure 4C), indicating that OXM acts primarily on the liver clock and in line with the observed phase stability of the SCN clock under time-restricted feeding conditions (Damiola et al., 2000).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of SCN response to OXM and comparison to literature on time-restricted feeding

claim: Phase delays of Per2 and Dbp mRNA rhythms were detected in livers of OXM-treated mice relative to those in PBS-injected control animals.
source: We detected phase delays of Per2 and Dbp mRNA rhythms in livers of OXM-treated mice relative to those in PBS-injected control animals (Figure 4D)
evidence: Based on experimental in vivo qPCR data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Per2, but not Dbp, rhythms appeared dampened after OXM injection.
source: In addition, Per2, but not Dbp, rhythms appeared dampened after OXM injection.
evidence: Based on experimental in vivo qPCR data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Transcript profiles of genes involved in liver carbohydrate metabolism (Foxo1 and Pdk4) were found phase delayed after OXM treatment.
source: Similar to what we observed for clock gene activity, transcript profiles of genes involved in liver carbohydrate metabolism were found either phase delayed (Foxo1 and Pdk4; Figure 5A,B)
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Transcript profiles of Foxo1 and Pklr were dampened after OXM treatment.
source: Similar to what we observed for clock gene activity, transcript profiles of genes involved in liver carbohydrate metabolism were found either phase delayed (Foxo1 and Pdk4; Figure 5A,B) and/or dampened (Foxo1 and Pklr; Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 5A,C

claim: Pepck was not rhythmic under the experimental conditions, and OXM had no further effect on Pepck mRNA levels.
source: Of note Pepck, which was previously described as a clock output gene in liver (Lamia et al., 2008) was not rhythmic under these conditions, and OXM had no further effect on Pepck mRNA levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Expression levels of the glucose transporter Slc2a2 (Glut2) and the pyruvate transporter Slc16a7 were dampened or phase-delayed, respectively, after OXM treatment.
source: Expression levels of the glucose transporter Slc2a2 (Glut2) and the pyruvate transporter Slc16a7 were also dampened or phase-delayed, respectively (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 5E,F

claim: In humans, OXM levels in the blood rise in response to food intake.
source: In humans, OXM levels in the blood rise in response to food intake (Le Quellec et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Le Quellec et al., 1992

claim: In fed mice, OLI levels were elevated during the active dark phase, while under fasting conditions OLI concentrations were constant and consistently low.
source: In fed mice, OLI levels were elevated during the active dark phase, while under fasting conditions OLI concentrations were constant and consistently low (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on experimental OLI measurement data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Non-rhythmic Gcg mRNA expression in the gut was observed under fasting conditions.
source: In line with this, non-rhythmic Gcg mRNA expression in the gut was observed under fasting conditions (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental data not shown in the manuscript

claim: Mean fasting OLI levels in the early morning (ZT1) were ∼3.5 ng/ml, but showed high inter-individual variation.
source: Mean fasting OLI levels in the early morning (ZT1) were ∼3.5 ng/ml, but showed high inter-individual variation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on experimental OLI measurement data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Upon food intake, a rapid increase in OLI (relative to individual fasting levels) was observed after 20 min, persisting for more than 1 hr before returning to baseline levels.
source: Upon food intake, a rapid increase (relative to individual fasting levels) was observed after 20 min. This effect persisted for more than 1 hr before returning to baseline levels (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on experimental OLI measurement data shown in Figure 6C

claim: OLI induction after OXM injections were about twofold–threefold higher than what was observed after refeeding.
source: Of note, OLI induction after OXM injections were about twofold–threefold higher than what was observed after refeeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental OLI measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Parallel to the rise in plasma OLI, a transient postprandial increase of hepatic Per1 expression was observed after fasting-refeeding.
source: Parallel to the rise in plasma OLI, we observed a transient postprandial increase of hepatic Per1 expression.
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Per2 expression showed a delayed, but a more persistent induction after fasting-refeeding.
source: Per2 expression showed a delayed, but a more persistent induction (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Food-mediated Per activation was partly inhibited by treatment with purified anti-OXM IgG to neutralize the effects of endogenous OXM in wild-type mice.
source: Food-mediated Per activation was partly inhibited by treatment with purified anti-OXM IgG to neutralize the effects of endogenous OXM in wild-type (Figure 6E)
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Food-mediated Per activation was partly inhibited by treatment with purified anti-OXM IgG in Glp1r−/− mice.
source: Food-mediated Per activation was partly inhibited by treatment with purified anti-OXM IgG to neutralize the effects of endogenous OXM in wild-type (Figure 6E) and in Glp1r−/− mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 6F

claim: The effects of refeeding on insulin, GLP-1, and GCG plasma levels were not affected by treatment with anti-OXM IgG.
source: Importantly, the effects of refeeding on insulin, GLP-1, and GCG plasma levels were not affected by treatment with anti-OXM IgG, suggesting that these peptides are not involved in the activation of food-induced hepatic Per expression (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: Based on experimental hormone measurement data shown in Figure 6G-I

claim: Insulin, GLP-1, and GCG are not involved in the activation of food-induced hepatic Per expression.
source: Importantly, the effects of refeeding on insulin, GLP-1, and GCG plasma levels were not affected by treatment with anti-OXM IgG, suggesting that these peptides are not involved in the activation of food-induced hepatic Per expression (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of anti-OXM IgG on these hormones while Per expression was affected

claim: After a 12-hr fast, food intake caused a significant phase delay of PER2::LUC activity in liver slices and this effect was attenuated by OXM neutralization.
source: After a 12-hr fast, food intake caused a significant phase delay of PER2::LUC activity in liver slices and this effect was attenuated by OXM neutralization (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: Based on experimental liver slice luminescence data shown in Figure 6J,K

claim: No effect on PER2::LUC phase was seen after anti-OXM treatment alone.
source: No effect on PER2::LUC phase was seen after anti-OXM treatment alone (Figure 6K).
evidence: Based on experimental liver slice luminescence data shown in Figure 6K

claim: Elevated OXM levels in response to food intake affect hepatic clock gene expression.
source: Together, these data suggest that elevated OXM levels in response to food intake affect hepatic clock gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing OXM induction by food and effects on clock genes

claim: Neutralization of endogenous OXM signaling inhibits food-induced clock gene induction and rhythm shifts.
source: Neutralization of endogenous OXM signaling inhibits food-induced clock gene induction and rhythm shifts, suggesting that OXM may act as a metabolic synchronizer of hepatic clocks.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing effects of anti-OXM antibody treatment

claim: OXM may act as a metabolic synchronizer of hepatic clocks.
source: Neutralization of endogenous OXM signaling inhibits food-induced clock gene induction and rhythm shifts, suggesting that OXM may act as a metabolic synchronizer of hepatic clocks.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results and speculative interpretation

claim: Eating during the normal rest phase leads to a state of internal circadian desynchrony which has been suggested to underlie metabolic deregulation under shiftwork conditions.
source: In consequence, eating during the normal rest phase leads to a state of internal circadian desynchrony which has been suggested to underlie metabolic deregulation under shiftwork conditions (Vollmers et al., 2009; Salgado-Delgado et al., 2010; Barclay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vollmers et al., 2009; Salgado-Delgado et al., 2010; Barclay et al., 2012

claim: Food entrainment does not exclusively depend on glucose.
source: However, food entrainment does not exclusively depend on glucose (Hirao et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirao et al., 2009

claim: In mice, food intake during day (the normal rest time) uncouples the liver clock from that in the SCN.
source: In mice, food intake during day (i.e., the normal rest time) uncouples the liver clock from that in the SCN (Lamia et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lamia et al., 2008

claim: Internal circadian desynchrony is associated with elevated body weight and other metabolic impairments.
source: leading to a state of internal circadian desynchrony that is associated with elevated body weight and other metabolic impairments (Arble et al., 2009; Hatori et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arble et al., 2009 and Hatori et al., 2012

claim: In the liver, around 10% of the transcriptome is under circadian regulation including many genes involved in energy metabolism.
source: In the liver, around 10% of the transcriptome is under circadian regulation including many genes involved in energy metabolism (Akhtar et al., 2002; Miller et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akhtar et al., 2002 and Miller et al., 2007

claim: Genetic ablation of the liver clock abolishes the circadian rhythms of several glucose regulatory genes and results in a perturbed diurnal profile of blood glucose.
source: Genetic ablation of the liver clock abolishes the circadian rhythms of several glucose regulatory genes and results in a perturbed diurnal profile of blood glucose (Kornmann et al., 2001; Lamia et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kornmann et al., 2001 and Lamia et al., 2008

claim: OXM displays a much greater capacity for clock gene induction in liver slices than GCG itself, despite having a lower binding affinity for GCGR.
source: This is puzzling given that OXM displays a much greater capacity for clock gene induction in liver slices than GCG itself, despite having a lower binding affinity for GCGR (LeSauter et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study and citation to LeSauter et al., 2009

claim: An additional OXM receptor has been suggested.
source: While our data suggest that GLP1R does not play a role in this context (Figures 2, 3), an additional OXM receptor has been suggested (Baldissera et al., 1988; Sun et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Baldissera et al., 1988 and Sun et al., 2015

claim: Insulin has previously been suggested to affect liver clock rhythms.
source: One such candidate could be insulin, which is similarly elevated after food intake and has previously been suggested to affect liver clock rhythms (Yamajuku et al., 2012; Chaves et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamajuku et al., 2012; Chaves et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015

claim: In response to food intake OXM levels go up, while GCG plasma concentrations are reduced.
source: In response to food intake OXM levels go up, while GCG plasma concentrations are reduced (Figure 6)
evidence: Based on experimental hormone measurement data shown in Figure 6

claim: GCG/GCGR signaling has recently been implicated in the regulation of hepatic Bmal1 expression in response to prolonged starvation.
source: Interestingly, GCG/GCGR signaling has recently been implicated in the regulation of hepatic Bmal1 expression in response to prolonged starvation (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2015

claim: Fasting-induced GCG signaling activates Bmal1 transcription via CREB/CRTC2 during the night.
source: Sun et al. show that fasting-induced GCG signaling activates Bmal1 transcription via CREB/CRTC2 during the night.
evidence: Supported by reference to Sun et al. findings

claim: GCGR signaling may have different clock targets depending on the time of activation.
source: As we did not observe any acute effects of OXM treatment on Bmal1 transcription (Figure 3), these data suggest that GCGR signaling may have different clock targets depending on the time of activation.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of OXM effects on Per genes vs. Bmal1 and comparison to Sun et al. findings

claim: GCGR activation is known to induce protein kinase A-mediated nuclear translocation and DNA-binding of phosphorylated CREB on target genes.
source: GCGR activation is known to induce protein kinase A-mediated nuclear translocation and DNA-binding of phosphorylated CREB on target genes (Gonzalez and Montminy, 1989; Dalle et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gonzalez and Montminy, 1989 and Dalle et al., 2004

claim: For various tissues—including the SCN—it has been shown that resetting of the circadian clock involves acute up-regulation of Per1 and Per2.
source: For various tissues—including the SCN—it has been shown that resetting of the circadian clock involves acute up-regulation of Per1 and Per2 (Dunlap, 1999; Lowrey and Takahashi, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dunlap, 1999 and Lowrey and Takahashi, 2004

claim: Per induction was observed after DEX treatment or serum shock in fibroblast and hepatoma cells.
source: Per induction was observed after DEX treatment or serum shock in fibroblast and hepatoma cells (Balsalobre et al., 1998, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Balsalobre et al., 1998, 2000

claim: Light pulses given during the dark phase induce CREB activation and Per expression in the SCN.
